title: Hiking in the Rain: 12 Essential Safety Tips for Kenya

meta_description: Hiking in the rain safety tips for Kenya's rainy seasons: flash floods, lightning, mud, river crossings, cold and what to wear on the trail.
excerpt: Practical hiking in the rain safety tips for Kenyan trails: how to plan around the long and short rains, avoid flash floods and lightning, handle mud and river crossings, prevent hypothermia and know when to turn back.

content:
Hiking in the rain safety tips start with three rules: check the forecast and turn back early, keep out of gorges and dry riverbeds when storms are about, and stay warm and dry with proper layers. In Kenya, rain itself is rarely the danger; flash floods, lightning, slippery ground and cold are.

Kenya's long rains (roughly March-May) and short rains (roughly October-December) do not have to stop you hiking, but they change the risks on every trail. This guide gives practical hiking in the rain safety tips for Kenyan conditions: how to plan, what to wear, how to handle mud, river crossings and thunderstorms, and when to call it a day.

Quick Facts

  • Rainy seasons: long rains roughly March-May, short rains roughly October-December
  • Timing: in the highlands, rain and storms often build in the afternoon, so start early
  • Biggest hazard: flash floods in gorges and dry riverbeds, even when it is not raining where you stand
  • Lightning rule: if thunder follows lightning within 30 seconds, get off high ground and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder
  • Cold risk: hypothermia can set in well above freezing when you are wet, tired and in the wind
  • Key gear: waterproof jacket, rain pants, grippy boots, a dry warm layer in a waterproof bag and a headlamp

Is It Safe to Go Hiking in the Rain?

Hiking in light or steady rain is safe on a familiar, well-marked trail if you are properly dressed and watch the weather. It becomes unsafe in thunderstorms, during heavy downpours near gorges or rivers, and when you are getting cold and cannot get dry.

The trick is to treat rain as a reason to plan more carefully, not a reason to stay home every weekend. The hiking in the rain safety tips below are grouped by the main hazards: flash floods, lightning, slippery ground, cold and poor visibility. Our rainy season hiking gear guide covers the kit side in more depth.

Which Kenyan trails are riskier in the rain?

Trails through narrow gorges, along riverbeds, on steep loose slopes or across exposed ridges are the riskiest in the rain. Hell's Gate's gorges, crater rims such as Mt Longonot and high moorland such as the Aberdares and Mt Kenya all need extra care in wet weather.

When hiking in the rain, remember that gorges can flood from rain that falls far upstream. In September 2019, a flash flood in a gorge at Hell's Gate National Park swept away a tour group and killed several people, and the Kenya Wildlife Service closed the gorge that day, as Al Jazeera reported. Steep volcanic trails like the one in our Mt Longonot hike guide turn slippery and loose when wet.

How Should You Plan a Hike in the Rainy Season?

Plan a rainy-season hike by checking the forecast the day before and the morning of the hike, starting early, choosing a shorter or lower route, and telling someone your plan and return time. Always set a turnaround time and keep to it.

Good planning is the most useful of all hiking in the rain safety tips, because most problems start with a late start or a route that was too ambitious for the conditions. Check the forecasts and advisories from the Kenya Meteorological Department, which issues seasonal outlooks and heavy-rain warnings for each region.

  1. Check the forecast for the hike area, not just Nairobi, the evening before and again at dawn.
  2. Start early, ideally on the trail by 7:00-8:00am, so you are heading down before afternoon storms build.
  3. Pick a route with a clear path, easy exit points and no river crossings or gorge sections.
  4. Share your route, group size and expected return time with someone at home.
  5. Set a turnaround time and agree with your group that anyone can call a retreat.
  6. Charge your phone, carry a headlamp and save the park or forest station contacts before you leave.

Should you hike with a group in the rain?

Hiking with a group or a guide is safer in the rain, because someone else can help if you slip, get cold or lose the path in mist. Experienced guides also know which sections flood or become dangerous after heavy rain.

If you are new to wet-weather hiking, a guided group hike lets you learn these hiking in the rain safety tips on the trail rather than the hard way. Our guide to hiking for beginners in Kenya explains how to build up to longer hikes.

What Are the Most Important Hiking in the Rain Safety Tips on the Trail?

The most important hiking in the rain safety tips on the trail are to keep out of gorges and riverbeds in storms, get off ridges when you hear thunder, slow down on slippery ground and add layers before you feel cold.

How do you stay safe from flash floods?

Stay safe from flash floods by avoiding gorges, narrow valleys and dry riverbeds whenever it is raining nearby or upstream. Signs of a coming flood include a sudden rise in water, muddy or debris-filled water and a roar from upstream.

If you notice any of these signs, climb to high ground straight away and do not go back for anything. Never camp or rest in a dry riverbed during the rainy season. Follow park ranger instructions on closures, because gorges and river sections may be shut after heavy rain for good reason.

What should you do if you are caught in a thunderstorm?

If you are caught in a thunderstorm, get off summits, ridges and open ground, move away from lone trees and water, and wait it out lower down. Spread your group out and crouch on your backpack with your feet together if lightning is very close.

The 30-30 rule helps you judge the danger when hiking in the rain: if thunder follows the flash within 30 seconds, lightning is close enough to strike, and you should wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before moving on. The American Hiking Society's lightning advice also warns against sheltering under rock overhangs or in shallow caves.

How do you walk safely on muddy, slippery trails?

Walk safely on muddy, slippery trails by shortening your stride, keeping your weight over your feet and placing each foot flat rather than on your heel. Trekking poles add two extra points of contact on descents.

Around Nairobi, black cotton soil turns sticky and slick after rain, and volcanic ash and scree slide underfoot. Avoid stepping on wet roots and smooth rock, and walk through puddles rather than on the slippery edges, which widens and damages the trail. Boots with deep lugs, such as a Quechua waterproof hiking boot, grip far better than trainers.

Is it safe to cross a river on a rainy-season hike?

Crossing a river in the rainy season is only safe when the water is clear, slow and below knee height. If it is fast, muddy or rising, do not cross; wait for it to drop or turn back.

When a crossing is safe, unbuckle your hip belt and chest strap so you can slip out of your pack if you fall, face upstream, move sideways one step at a time and use trekking poles or a partner for balance. Look downstream before you start for rapids, waterfalls or fallen trees.

What Should You Wear for Hiking in the Rain?

For hiking in the rain, wear a breathable waterproof jacket, rain pants, quick-drying synthetic or wool layers, and boots with a deep tread. Pack a dry warm layer and spare socks in a waterproof bag, and avoid cotton completely.

Clothing is where hiking in the rain safety tips and comfort overlap: wet cotton jeans and hoodies stay cold and heavy for hours, while synthetics and wool keep you warmer when damp. Our waterproof rain pants guide and our guide to what to wear hiking in Kenya explain each layer in detail.

How Do You Avoid Hypothermia When Hiking in the Rain?

Avoid hypothermia by staying dry, adding layers before you feel cold, eating and drinking regularly and getting out of the wind when you stop. Hypothermia does not need freezing temperatures; wet clothing and wind can chill you on any high Kenyan trail.

When hiking in the rain, watch your group for the early warning signs, often called the "umbles": stumbling, mumbling, fumbling and grumbling, along with constant shivering and unusual tiredness. People who are getting hypothermic often do not notice it themselves.

If someone shows these signs, get them out of the wind and rain, replace wet layers with dry ones, insulate them from the ground and give warm, sweet drinks and food if they can swallow. If shivering stops, they cannot walk or they do not improve, call for help early. On the Aberdares or Mt Kenya, where cold rain is common, these hiking in the rain safety tips matter most.

Pro Tips: Rainy Day Hiking Checklist

  • Start early: aim to be descending before afternoon storms build
  • Turnaround time: agree on it before you set off and keep to it
  • Dry layer: keep a fleece and spare socks in a waterproof bag
  • Phone protection: use a zip-lock bag or dry pouch and keep the battery charged
  • Snacks on hand: eat little and often to keep warm
  • No gorges in storms: stay out of gorges and riverbeds when rain is falling upstream

When Should You Turn Back or Cancel a Hike?

Turn back or cancel a hike when heavy rain or thunderstorms are forecast for the area, when rivers on your route are rising, when anyone in the group is getting cold or when mist hides the trail markers.

Turning back is one of the hardest but most valuable hiking in the rain safety tips to follow, because the summit or waterfall will still be there next weekend. Decide on clear turnaround triggers before you start, so nobody feels pressured on the day. If roads to the trailhead are flooded or impassable, cancel; getting stuck on a muddy murram road is a common rainy-season problem.

After hiking in the rain, dry your boots away from direct heat, hang your waterproofs to air, and check for any cuts or blisters. Our rain jackets for hiking in Nairobi guide explains how to keep your waterproofs working for many seasons.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can you hike in Kenya during the rainy season?

You can hike in Kenya during the rainy season if you choose suitable trails and follow sensible hiking in the rain safety tips. Rain in the highlands often falls in the afternoon, so early starts help. Avoid gorges, river crossings and long exposed ridges during storms, and check park closures with KWS or KFS before you go.

What should you not do when hiking in the rain?

When hiking in the rain, do not wear cotton, enter gorges or dry riverbeds, cross fast or rising rivers, or stay on summits and ridges during thunder. Do not shelter under lone trees or rock overhangs in lightning, and do not push on past your turnaround time because the weather might clear.

Is it dangerous to hike in a thunderstorm?

Hiking in a thunderstorm is dangerous on summits, ridges and open ground, because lightning tends to strike high points. If thunder follows lightning within 30 seconds, get lower, move away from tall isolated objects and water, and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before continuing. Plan early starts to avoid afternoon storms.

How do you keep your phone and gear dry when hiking in the rain?

Keep your phone and gear dry by packing everything important in waterproof dry bags or zip-lock bags inside your backpack, and using a rain cover over the pack. A heavy-duty bin bag makes a cheap liner. Keep your phone in a sealed pouch in an inside pocket so it stays dry and close to hand.

Do you need waterproof boots for hiking in the rain?

Waterproof boots help keep your feet dry in light rain and mud, but grip matters more than waterproofing. Deep lugs hold better on wet rock and black cotton soil. In very heavy rain water can still enter over the top, so wear gaiters, carry spare wool socks and dry your boots after each hike.

Final Thoughts

The best hiking in the rain safety tips are simple: check the forecast, start early, stay out of gorges and riverbeds in storms, get off high ground when thunder is close, and keep warm and dry with proper layers. With good planning, Kenya's rainy seasons offer green, quiet trails.
